title: The dance on the serpent's hoods
hookLine: free of the coils, Krishna climbs onto the serpent's hoods and dances until his pride is gone
carry: he humbles the ego and spares the soul
tomorrow: Spared by the feet that humbled him

lines: HE SEES THE GRIEF ON THE BANK.
cards: Why does he go still? In the Bhagavata's telling, he isn't overpowered. It turns to the bank: his mother, his friends, the cows, all stricken.
Krishna sees what his stillness is doing to the people who love him. He has stayed bound, playing the part of a mortal, the text says, only for a short time. Now he decides that's enough.

teach.h: HE GROWS, AND THE COILS LET GO.
teach.b: Krishna makes his body grow. The coils, holding a small boy, are suddenly stretched around something they can't contain, and Kaliya has to let go.

The serpent rears up, hissing, eyes burning, breath smoking with poison, and the two circle in the water, Krishna moving around him the way Garuda, the great eagle, circles a snake, until Kaliya is worn out.
He presses down the raised hoods, climbs onto them, and begins to dance. Celestial musicians gather, and drums, songs and flowers come down from the sky.
Whichever hood Kaliya lifts, Krishna's feet come down on it, keeping time. Kaliya thrashes, then weakens. Blood comes from his mouths.
His hoods are broken, his pride with them.
And at last, exhausted, the serpent turns his mind toward the one dancing on him and, the text says, remembers the ancient Lord. What Krishna leaves undone matters. He doesn't kill Kaliya.
The fight becomes a dance, and the dance goes on until the pride is gone and the serpent remembers God.

teach.h: THE EGO HUMBLED, THE SOUL SPARED.
teach.b: Many teachers read Kaliya as the ego, ahankara in Sanskrit, the sense of me first that rears a new head every time you press one down, and its poison as what it puts into a life.

In that reading, Krishna doesn't destroy the one who carries the ego. He dances it down, and what's left turns toward him. Hindus know the scene as Kaliya-mardana: a small boy, one foot raised, on a cobra's hood.

how: Krishna dancing on Kaliya's hoods, Kaliya-mardana, appears in temple sculpture, bronzes, paintings and classical dance, and devotees tell it among the stories of Krishna's childhood in Vraja.

o: the celestial drummer who plays for the dance
the great eagle who circles snakes in the water
the serpent whose pride is danced out on his own hoods

games.q: the dance on the hoods — tap the pairs.
p: grows until the coils let go
the ego, as many read Kaliya

s: Krishna kills Kaliya in the pool
he dances on the hoods until the serpent's pride is broken, and spares him.
music and flowers come down while he dances
the text stages it as a celestial performance.
Kaliya, worn out, remembers the Lord
exhausted, he turns his mind to the one dancing on him.

games.q: you're Krishna, free of the coils, and the serpent rears up in front of you, hissing poison. what do you do?
o: strike him dead with one blow.
climb onto his hoods and dance.
games.why: he dances until the serpent's pride is gone, and spares him. many read the hoods as the ego: humbled, not destroyed.

practice: Many Hindus end a prayer by bowing all the way down, a pranam, forehead to the floor. The head goes lowest, the part of us that most likes to rear up. Kneel or sit, and lower your head as far as is comfortable.
Bring to mind where your pride has been rearing up lately. With each breath out, let it come down a little, the way Kaliya's hoods came down. If you pray, offer it to God.
If you don't, simply rest there a moment, low and quiet.

wordCard.voice: Kaliya. The serpent whose coils can't hold the growing boy, and whose pride is danced out of him on his own hoods.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Kaliya, the serpent Krishna dances on.
